lesson.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

goalMatch.note: This video covers exactly what you need: how to rebase a branch onto main and how to resolve conflicts, with a worked example.

sources.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts

steps.title: Recreate the conflicting example repo
steps.instructions: In an empty folder run `git init -b main`, commit app.txt (title/body/footer), then `git switch -c feature/login` and make three commits (line 1 -> Login title, add login.txt, line 3 -> Login footer). Switch back with `git switch main`, make two commits changing line 1 and line 3, then run `git branch -a` to confirm the feature branch has no remote copy.

precision_checks.label: Branches have diverged
precision_checks.command: test "$(git rev-list --count main..feature/login)" -ge 1 && test "$(git rev-list --count feature/login..main)" -ge 1

targets.caption: git branch -a lists only local branches, so the feature branch is safe to rebase

explanations.topic: Use git branch -a to check whether the feature branch was pushed
Conflicts during rebase: abort or fix them while rebasing
Rebase replays commits one by one, so each can conflict
Example layout: 3 feature commits, 2 new main commits

hints: Make each change on its own line and commit after each edit.
Branch off with git switch -c feature/login before editing, then return with git switch main.
On main, only touch lines 1 and 3 so they clash with the feature commits; leave login.txt only on the feature branch.
Run git branch -a: if no remotes/ entries appear, the branch was never pushed.
common_mistakes: Making main's commits before creating the feature branch, so there is no divergence
Forgetting to git add before committing, leaving changes uncommitted
Editing the same line on both branches identically so no conflict arises
Running in a folder that already has a .git repo or remote
steps.code:
git init -b main
printf 'title\nbody\nfooter\n' > app.txt
git add app.txt && git commit -m "Initial app"
git switch -c feature/login
# commit 1: line 1 -> Login title
# commit 2: add login.txt
# commit 3: line 3 -> Login footer
git switch main
# commit 1: line 1 -> Main title
# commit 2: line 3 -> Main footer
git branch -a

steps.title: Start the rebase onto main
steps.instructions: Run `git switch feature/login` and then `git rebase main`; it stops with a CONFLICT in app.txt. Run `git status` to confirm a rebase is in progress.

targets.caption: Rebase pauses on the first conflicting commit
git status confirms the rebase is paused

explanations.topic: A rebase pauses when a reapplied commit conflicts
git status shows which commit failed and how many remain
Fixing rebase conflicts works like merge conflicts: Git inserts conflict markers

hints: Make sure you are on the feature branch before rebasing; git rebase main replays the current branch onto main.
A CONFLICT message here is expected, not an error: the repo was set up to conflict.
Run git status to see 'rebase in progress' and the list of remaining commands.
If you are on main, run git switch feature/login (or your branch name) first.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase main while still on main, which reports 'Current branch main is up to date'
Running git rebase --abort in panic after seeing CONFLICT
Running git merge main instead of git rebase main
Skipping the conflict setup in step 1, so the rebase succeeds without conflicts
steps.code:
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
git status

steps.title: Resolve the first conflict
steps.instructions: Open app.txt, delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers and keep the line that should stay. Stage it with `git add app.txt` and run `git status`.

targets.caption: Open the conflicted file and remove the conflict markers

explanations.topic: Remove markers and keep the code that should stay
Run git add on every conflicted file once fixed
Rebase uses git rebase --continue instead of git commit

hints: Open app.txt in your editor and look for the lines starting with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>.
Delete all three marker lines and keep only the content that should remain after the rebase.
Save the file, then run `git add app.txt` to mark the conflict as resolved.
Run `git status` to confirm no files are still listed as 'both modified'.
common_mistakes: Leaving one of the marker lines (often =======) in the file.
Forgetting to save the file before running git add.
Running git commit instead of staging and then continuing the rebase.
Keeping both versions of the line when only one should stay.

steps.title: Continue the rebase
steps.instructions: Run `git rebase --continue` and save the commit message in vim with Escape, `:wq`, Enter. Git applies the next non-conflicting commit, then pauses again on the next conflict in your file.

targets.caption: Continue the rebase instead of committing
Git pauses again on the next conflict

explanations.topic: Git opens vim to edit the commit message
Exiting vim with Escape then :wq keeps the message
Rebase pauses again when the next commit conflicts
The third commit conflicts again, so the rebase pauses once more

hints: Make sure every resolved file has been staged with git add before continuing.
Run git rebase --continue, not git commit, to move to the next commit.
If vim opens, press Escape, type :wq and press Enter to keep the commit message.
Seeing a new CONFLICT message is expected here: the third commit conflicts again.
common_mistakes: Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue
Getting stuck in vim by typing text before pressing Escape, or typing wq without the colon
Running git rebase --continue before staging the resolved file with git add
Leaving conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) in the file before continuing
Treating the new conflict as an error and aborting the rebase

steps.title: Fix last conflict and finish
steps.instructions: Remove the conflict markers in app.txt, run `git add app.txt`, then `git rebase --continue` and save with `:wq`. Run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph` to confirm your commits now sit on top of main.

targets.caption: git status shows no rebase in progress

explanations.topic: With no commits left, --continue concludes the rebase
Use git status to confirm you're out of the rebasing state

hints: Fix this conflict exactly the way you fixed the first one.
Open app.txt, delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines, and keep the content you want.
Run git add app.txt, then git rebase --continue, and type :wq in the editor to save the commit message.
Run git status. It should say 'On branch ...' with no rebase in progress. git log --oneline --graph should show your commits on top of main.
common_mistakes: Leaving a ======= or >>>>>>> line in app.txt and committing it.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue.
Forgetting to git add app.txt before continuing, so git reports unresolved conflicts.
Quitting vim with :q! instead of :wq, which aborts the commit message.
Running git rebase --skip and losing the third commit.
steps.code:
(conflict markers <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> removed from app.txt, keeping the combined content)
git add app.txt
git rebase --continue
:wq
git status
git log --oneline --graph
